summary: Shares observations on implementations of POP3, the Post Office Protocol. It is informational and does not define a protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo records differences between POP3 implementations. It shows how client expectations can affect compatibility even when the protocol does not require them.

questions: what issues arise in pop3 implementations
why did pop3 clients expect a space
subtitle: Implementation observations about POP3 server and client behavior.

tldr.problem: POP3 clients sometimes depend on behavior that the protocol specification does not require, and optional commands can become practical dependencies.
tldr.mechanism: The memo records observations about response formatting, UIDL, TOP, and APOP in POP3 implementations.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1957 updates RFC 1939 with these observations; it is informational and does not define a new protocol.

today: RFC 1957 updates RFC 1939 and records implementation observations. The unit metadata lists no later update to RFC 1957.

sections.title: Implementation Differences
sections.content:
RFC 1957 warns that a widely used implementation can be mistaken for the standard. It reports cases where POP3 clients expected particular server behavior that RFC 1939 did not require.

The memo documents these observations for people implementing or maintaining POP3 software. It does not specify an Internet standard.
sections.plainLanguage: Software can develop habits that the written rules never required. This memo describes several such habits in POP3.

sections.title: Space After the Status Indicator
sections.content:
The UCB POP3 server called popper always placed a space after its status indicator. Two clients were observed to expect that space and fail when it was absent, although RFC 1939 did not require it.

The client authors were contacted, and new releases would not expect the space. The memo says old versions should still be supported.
sections.plainLanguage: Some clients failed unless a server included an extra space. The protocol rules did not require the space, but older clients still needed support.

sections.title: Optional Commands and APOP
sections.content:
The memo reports that Netscape required the optional UIDL command and Eudora required the optional TOP command. This illustrates how a feature marked optional in a specification may still matter for compatibility with a particular client.

It also says APOP had not achieved wide penetration at the time. The memo lists some server and client implementations that supported APOP.
sections.plainLanguage: Some clients depended on commands labeled optional. The memo also notes that APOP support existed but was not widespread at the time.

references.text: Myers, J., and M. Rose, "Post Office Protocol - Version 3", STD 53, RFC 1939, May 1996.
